title: Volcanoes Under the Sea
summary: How most of Earth's volcanoes erupt hidden under the ocean, building new seafloor, seamounts and islands, feeding strange life at hot vents, and slowly widening the Red Sea.
poll: Exploring the deep sea is just as important as exploring space.

versions.title: Fire Under the Sea
versions.text:
Most volcanoes are not on land. They are deep in the sea. We do not see them.

A volcano is a hole in the ground. Hot rock comes up. It is soft. It is magma. When it comes out, it is lava.

The sea floor can split. Magma comes up in the crack. It cools. It makes new floor. This goes on all the time.

The sea is cold. It cools the lava fast. The lava makes round lumps. They look like big pillows!

Some grow and grow. At last they poke out. Then they make an island. Hawaii was made this way.

Some spots are like hot springs. They are vents. Hot water shoots out. It looks like black smoke. Odd worms and crabs live there. It is dark there.

The Red Sea has a crack, too. It is in the middle. The sea gets a bit wider each year.

versions.title: Fire Under the Sea
versions.text:
Most volcanoes on Earth are not on land. They are deep under the sea. We cannot see them. But they are there.

A volcano is a place where hot rock comes up from deep in the Earth. The hot, melted rock is called magma. When it comes out, it is called lava.

In some parts of the sea, the floor splits. Magma rises up into the crack. It cools and turns into new sea floor. This goes on all the time.

Sea water is very cold. It cools the lava fast. The lava forms round lumps. They look like big pillows.

Some sea volcanoes keep on growing. They can get so tall that their tops come out of the water. Then they make an island. The islands of Hawaii were made this way.

Some spots on the sea floor are like hot springs. They are called vents. Very hot water rushes out. It looks like black smoke. Strange worms, crabs, and clams live near the vents. They live in the dark.

The Red Sea has a crack down its middle, too. The sea gets a bit wider each year.

versions.title: Volcanoes Under the Sea
versions.text:
Most volcanoes on Earth are not on land. They are hidden deep under the sea. People cannot see them. But they erupt all the time.

A volcano is a place where hot rock comes up from deep in the Earth. The hot, melted rock is called magma. When magma comes out of the ground, it is called lava.

In some places, the sea floor is slowly splitting apart. Magma rises up into the cracks. It cools and becomes new sea floor. The cracks make a long chain of mountains under the sea.

Sea water is very cold. It cools the lava fast. The lava gets hard in round lumps that look like pillows.

Some sea volcanoes grow for a very long time. They can get so tall that they rise out of the water. Then they become an island. The islands of Hawaii were made this way.

The sea floor also has vents. They are like hot springs. Very hot water rushes out. It is full of minerals and looks like black smoke. Strange worms, crabs, and clams live near the vents. No sunlight gets down there.

The Red Sea has a crack down its middle, too. The floor is splitting, so the Red Sea gets a little wider each year.

versions.title: Volcanoes Under the Sea
versions.text:
When people think of a volcano, they picture a tall mountain with smoke on top. But most volcanoes on Earth are hidden deep under the sea. In fact, most eruptions on our planet happen underwater. No one sees them.

A volcano forms where hot rock rises from deep inside the Earth. This hot, melted rock is called magma. When magma comes out of the ground, it is called lava.

In some places, the sea floor is slowly pulling apart. Magma rises into the cracks. It cools and becomes new sea floor. These cracks form the longest chain of mountains on Earth, and almost all of it is underwater.

Sea water is very cold, so it cools the lava fast. The lava gets hard in round lumps. Scientists call it pillow lava.

Some sea volcanoes keep growing for thousands of years. A few grow so tall that they rise out of the water and become an island. The islands of Hawaii were built this way.

The sea floor also has vents, which are like hot springs. Very hot water rushes out. It is full of minerals that look like black smoke. Tube worms, crabs, and clams live near the vents. Sunlight never reaches them.

The Red Sea has a crack down its middle, too. As the floor splits, the Red Sea gets a little wider each year.

versions.title: Hidden Volcanoes of the Deep
versions.text:
When most people think of a volcano, they picture a tall mountain with smoke rising from its top. Yet most of the volcanoes on Earth are hidden deep under the ocean. Scientists think that most eruptions on our planet happen underwater. Nobody sees them.

A volcano forms where hot, melted rock called magma rises from deep inside the Earth. When magma pours out onto the surface, it is called lava.

In some parts of the ocean, the seafloor is slowly pulling apart. Magma rises into the gap. It cools and becomes new seafloor. These cracks form a long ridge that winds around the whole planet like the seam on a ball. It is the longest mountain chain on Earth.

Deep water also changes how an eruption looks. The weight of the water above makes huge pressure. So most deep eruptions are quiet, not explosive. The cold water cools the lava so fast that it forms round lumps called pillow lava.

Underwater volcanoes that grow into mountains are called seamounts. A few grow tall enough to break through the surface and become islands. The islands of Hawaii were built this way, one eruption at a time.

The seafloor also has vents, which work like hot springs. Water hotter than boiling shoots out. It carries dark minerals that look like smoke. Tube worms, crabs, and clams live around these vents in total darkness.

The Red Sea sits on a crack, too. As the seafloor splits, the Red Sea grows a little wider every year.

versions.title: Hidden Volcanoes of the Deep
versions.text:
When most people imagine a volcano, they picture a tall mountain with smoke curling from its top. However, most of the volcanoes on Earth are hidden far beneath the ocean. Scientists think that most eruptions on our planet take place underwater, where nobody can watch them.

A volcano forms where hot, melted rock called magma rises from deep inside the Earth. Once magma flows out onto the surface, it is called lava.

In some parts of the ocean, the seafloor is slowly pulling apart. Magma rises into the gap, cools, and hardens into brand-new seafloor. These cracks form an underwater ridge that winds around the whole planet like the seam on a baseball. It is the longest mountain range on Earth. It stretches for tens of thousands of kilometers.

Deep water also changes the way an eruption behaves. The heavy water above creates enormous pressure, so most deep eruptions are gentle, not explosive. The cold water cools the lava so quickly that it forms round lumps known as pillow lava.

Underwater volcanoes that grow into mountains are called seamounts. A few become tall enough to break through the surface and form islands. The islands of Hawaii were built this way, eruption after eruption.

The seafloor also has vents, which act like hot springs. Scalding water rushes out. It carries dark minerals that look like smoke. Tube worms, crabs, and clams survive around these vents in complete darkness.

The Red Sea lies on one of these cracks. As the seafloor splits, the Red Sea becomes a little wider every year.

versions.title: Volcanoes Beneath the Waves
versions.text:
When most people imagine a volcano, they picture a towering mountain with smoke curling from its top. However, most of the volcanoes on Earth are hidden far beneath the ocean. Scientists estimate that most of the eruptions on our planet take place underwater, where they are almost never seen.

A volcano forms wherever hot, melted rock called magma rises from deep inside the Earth. Once magma flows out onto the surface, it is called lava.

In certain parts of the ocean, the seafloor is slowly separating. Magma rises into the widening gap, cools, and hardens into brand-new seafloor. These cracks form an underwater ridge that winds around the entire planet like the stitching on a baseball. It is the longest mountain range on Earth, stretching tens of thousands of kilometers.

The deep ocean also changes the way an eruption behaves. The great weight of the water above creates enormous pressure, so most deep eruptions are gentle rather than explosive. Meanwhile, the icy water cools the lava so rapidly that it forms rounded lumps known as pillow lava.

Underwater volcanoes that grow into mountains are called seamounts. A few finally become tall enough to break through the surface and form islands. The Hawaiian Islands were built this way, one eruption after another.

The seafloor also contains vents, which behave like underwater hot springs. Scalding water gushes out, carrying dissolved minerals that look like black smoke. Amazingly, tube worms, crabs, and clams survive around these vents in complete darkness.

The Red Sea lies right on top of one of these cracks. As the seafloor keeps splitting, the Red Sea becomes slightly wider every year.

versions.title: Volcanoes Beneath the Waves
versions.text:
When most people imagine a volcano, they picture a towering mountain with smoke curling from its summit. However, the majority of the volcanoes on Earth are concealed far beneath the ocean. Scientists estimate that most of the eruptions on our planet take place underwater, where they are almost never observed.

A volcano forms wherever hot, melted rock called magma rises from deep inside the Earth. Once magma escapes onto the surface, it is called lava.

In certain regions of the ocean, the seafloor is gradually separating. Magma rises into the widening gap, cools, and hardens into brand-new seafloor. Together, these cracks form an underwater ridge that winds around the entire planet like the stitching on a baseball, making it the longest mountain range on Earth.

The deep ocean also changes the way an eruption behaves. Because the tremendous weight of the water above creates enormous pressure, most deep eruptions are gentle rather than explosive. Meanwhile, the frigid water cools the lava so rapidly that it forms rounded lumps known as pillow lava.

Underwater volcanoes that grow into mountains are called seamounts. A few eventually become tall enough to break through the surface and form islands. That is exactly how the Hawaiian Islands were built, one eruption after another.

The seafloor also contains vents, which work like underwater hot springs. Scalding water gushes out, carrying dissolved minerals that resemble black smoke. Remarkably, tube worms, crabs, and clams survive around these vents in complete darkness, even though no sunlight ever reaches them.

The Red Sea lies directly above one of these cracks. As the seafloor continues to separate, the Red Sea becomes slightly wider every year.

versions.title: The Secret Volcanoes of the Ocean Floor
versions.text:
When most people imagine a volcano, they picture a towering mountain with smoke curling from its summit. However, the majority of Earth's volcanoes are concealed beneath the ocean, and scientists estimate that most of the eruptions on our planet occur underwater, where they are rarely witnessed.

A volcano forms wherever magma, which is molten rock, rises through the crust, the thin outer layer of the Earth. Once magma escapes onto the surface, it is called lava.

The crust is broken into enormous tectonic plates that move extremely slowly. In certain regions of the ocean, two plates are gradually separating, and magma rises into the widening gap, where it cools and hardens into brand-new seafloor. Together, these boundaries form a mid-ocean ridge that winds around the entire planet like the stitching on a baseball, creating the longest mountain range on Earth.

The deep ocean also transforms the way an eruption behaves. Because the tremendous weight of the water creates enormous pressure, most deep eruptions are relatively gentle, and the frigid water cools the lava so rapidly that it forms rounded lumps known as pillow lava. Shallow underwater volcanoes can be considerably more violent, however: in 2022, the Hunga Tonga volcano in the Pacific exploded so powerfully that it triggered a tsunami that crossed the ocean.

Underwater volcanoes that grow into mountains are called seamounts, and a few eventually break through the surface to form islands. The Hawaiian Islands were built this way. In 1963, sailors near Iceland watched a brand-new island, later named Surtsey, rise out of the sea in a cloud of steam and ash.

The seafloor also contains hydrothermal vents, which work like underwater hot springs. Scalding water gushes out, carrying dissolved minerals that resemble black smoke. Remarkably, tube worms, crabs, and clams thrive there in complete darkness. Scientists study these places using a submersible, a small vessel built to withstand the crushing depths.

The Red Sea lies directly above a spreading boundary, so it becomes slightly wider every year.

Collectively, these boundaries form a mid-ocean ridge that winds around the entire planet like the stitching on a baseball, constituting the longest mountain range on Earth.

The deep ocean also fundamentally transforms the way an eruption behaves. Because the tremendous weight of the overlying water generates enormous pressure, most deep eruptions are relatively gentle, and the frigid water cools the lava so rapidly that it solidifies into rounded formations known as pillow lava. Shallow underwater volcanoes, however, can be extraordinarily violent. A hydrothermal vent was discovered for the first time.
questions.why: The article says sailors near Iceland saw a brand-new island, later named Surtsey, rise from the sea in 1963.

wrong.A: The tsunami in the article came from Hunga Tonga in 2022, in the Pacific.
wrong.B: The article does not say when submersibles were invented.
wrong.D: The article does not date the discovery of vents.

questions.stem: How do deep underwater eruptions compare with some shallow ones?
options: Deep eruptions are usually gentle, while shallow ones can be extremely violent.
Deep eruptions are more explosive because the water is colder.
Both kinds are always silent and harmless.
Shallow eruptions only produce pillow lava.
questions.why: The article says enormous pressure keeps most deep eruptions gentle, but shallow volcanoes such as Hunga Tonga can be extraordinarily violent.

wrong.B: Pressure makes deep eruptions gentler, not more explosive.
wrong.C: The Hunga Tonga eruption caused a tsunami, so they are not always harmless.
wrong.D: Pillow lava is linked to cold deep water, not described as the only product of shallow eruptions.

questions.stem: What does the Hunga Tonga eruption suggest about shallow underwater volcanoes?
options: They are always too small to notice.
They only affect the deep seafloor.
They build islands without any danger.
They can endanger coasts far across the ocean.
questions.why: Its blast produced a tsunami that traveled across the ocean, so a shallow eruption can threaten places far away.

wrong.A: An eruption that causes an ocean-crossing tsunami is not small.
wrong.B: Its effects reached across the ocean, not just the seafloor.
wrong.C: The article describes it as violent, not harmless.

questions.stem: Why do scientists need a submersible to study hydrothermal vents?
options: Vents are found only in shallow water near sandy beaches.
Submersibles are the only tool that can cool the scalding vent water.
The vents lie at crushing depths that people cannot reach unprotected.
Tube worms attack any divers who swim too close to them.
questions.why: The article says vents are in the deep ocean, where pressure is enormous, and a submersible is built to withstand those depths.

wrong.A: The vents are on the deep seafloor, not near beaches.
wrong.D: The article does not say tube worms attack anyone.
wrong.B: A submersible protects scientists; it does not cool the water.

questions.stem: The article says most of Earth's volcanoes are concealed beneath the ocean. What does concealed mean?
options: Destroyed
Hidden from view
Frozen solid by cold water
Growing quickly
questions.why: The volcanoes are under the ocean, where people rarely see them, so concealed means hidden.

wrong.A: The volcanoes are active, not destroyed.
wrong.C: The water is cold, but the volcanoes are not frozen.
wrong.D: Concealed describes being out of sight, not speed of growth.

questions.stem: Why does the author end the article with the Red Sea?
options: To show that the process of plates spreading apart is happening today, close to Saudi Arabia
To argue that the Red Sea is more important than the Pacific
To warn readers that a tsunami will soon hit the Red Sea
To explain how tube worms reached the Red Sea
questions.why: By noting that the Red Sea sits on a spreading boundary and widens each year, the author connects the science to a nearby, ongoing example.

wrong.B: The article does not rank seas by importance.
wrong.C: The article gives no tsunami warning for the Red Sea.
wrong.D: The article does not discuss tube worms in the Red Sea.

HIGH.prompt: Scientists say we know less about the deep seafloor than about the surface of the Moon. Using evidence from the article, explain why studying underwater volcanoes is important.
checklist: I stated a clear claim about why this research matters.
I supported it with at least three pieces of evidence from the article.
I used precise vocabulary such as tectonic, hydrothermal, or submersible.
